title: Per-key order at scale
summary: Detect out-of-order and duplicate events with versions, process keys in parallel inside one consumer without breaking their order, commit only what is safe, and know how Service Bus sessions and SQS FIFO groups do the same.

steps.title: Versions catch what ordering cannot
body: Even with a good key, events arrive out of order in real systems: a producer retry without idempotence, a replay, two
producers for one entity, a requeue, a migration that re-sends history. The robust fix is in the **data**: every event
carries the entity's **version** (or a per-entity sequence number) and the consumer remembers the last version it
applied per key.
- `version <= last`: **stale or duplicate**, skip it (and count it in a metric).
- `version == last + 1`: apply it.
- `version > last + 1`: a **gap**. If events are full snapshots ("status is now delivered") you can apply and move on;
if they are deltas ("add 5 to stock") you must wait for the missing one, park the event, or reload state from the
source.
Store the last version **in the same transaction** as the state it protects (a `version` column with
`UPDATE ... WHERE id = @id AND version = @expected`), so the check and the write cannot race.
Step through the program: the late `v2` cannot overwrite `delivered`.

code: var events = new (string Key, long Version, string Status)[] { ("A1", 1, "packed"), ("A1", 3, "delivered"), ("A1", 2, "shipped") };

steps.prompt: One key's events arrive with these versions. What does this print?
explain: The duplicate `2` is skipped, `4` opens a gap and is applied, so the late `3` is now stale and skipped too. For
snapshot events that is correct. For delta events `3` is lost: those need the gap handled (wait or reload), which the
boss of this module asks for.

steps.title: A version gate
prompt: Write a class `VersionGate` that a consumer calls before applying an event.
- `string Apply(string key, long version)`, versions start at 1 for every key:
- `version <= last` → `"stale (have v{last})"`, nothing changes;
- `version == last + 1` → remember it, return `"applied"`;
- `version > last + 1` → `"gap (expected v{last + 1})"`, nothing changes (the caller parks the event).
- `long Version(string key)`: the last applied version (0 for an unknown key).
starter: public string Apply(string key, long version) => "";
solution: public string Apply(string key, long version)
hints: `last.GetValueOrDefault(key)` is 0 for a key you have not seen.
Check stale first, then gap, then apply.
template: Dojo.Eq("v1 of a new key", "applied", dojoG.Apply("A1", 1));
Dojo.Eq("a duplicate is stale", "stale (have v2)", dojoG.Apply("A1", 2));
Dojo.Eq("an old replay is stale", "stale (have v2)", dojoG.Apply("A1", 1));
Dojo.Eq("a gap is reported, not applied", "gap (expected v3)", dojoG.Apply("A1", 4));
Dojo.Eq("a key that starts with a gap", "gap (expected v1)", dojoG.Apply("C4", 2));
Dojo.Eq("unknown key is at v0", 0L, dojoG.Version("zz"));

steps.title: Parallel inside one consumer, ordered per key
body: One partition, one consumer: with a 20 ms database call per record that is 50 records per second, whatever the
partition count. To go faster **without breaking per-key order**, dispatch inside the consumer by key:
```text
consume loop (one thread, offset order)
| worker = stableHash(key) % 2
v                           v
(one key always on one worker, so its events stay in order)
done: 101 103 104 ......  in flight: 100  ->  safe to commit: 100  (not 105!)
- Same key, same worker: per-key order holds; different keys run in parallel.
- **Commit only below the lowest offset still in flight.** If 101 to 104 are done but 100 is not, committing 105
and then crashing loses 100. Track in-flight offsets per partition and commit the smallest one.
- Use **bounded** queues per worker (`Channel.CreateBounded<T>(capacity)`) so a slow worker slows the consume loop
instead of filling memory; stop dispatching for partitions you lose in the revoke handler.
- In .NET the building blocks are `System.Threading.Channels` and `Task`s; in Java the Confluent Parallel Consumer
library does exactly this.
```csharp
var workers = Enumerable.Range(0, 8).Select(_ => Channel.CreateBounded<ConsumeResult<string, string>>(100)).ToArray();
foreach (var ch in workers)
_ = Task.Run(async () =>
await foreach (var cr in ch.Reader.ReadAllAsync(ct)) { await HandleAsync(cr); tracker.Done(cr.Offset.Value); }

options: Events of the same key can be handled concurrently or out of order

It makes each record be handled twice

steps.prompt: Arrange the consume loop of a key-dispatching consumer (one partition).
explain: The offset must be marked as started **before** the record reaches a worker, otherwise a fast worker could report
it done before the tracker knows it exists, and the commit position would jump past it.

steps.title: Track the safe commit position
prompt: Write a class `OffsetTracker` for one partition whose records are processed in parallel.
- `void Started(long offset)`: the record was handed to a worker.
- `void Done(long offset)`: the worker finished it (offsets finish in any order).
- `long? Committable`: the offset to commit, meaning "everything below this is done":
- `null` while nothing has finished yet;
- the **smallest offset still in flight**, if any;
- otherwise the highest finished offset + 1.
solution: if (maxDone is null || offset > maxDone) maxDone = offset;
hints: A `SortedSet<long>` of in-flight offsets gives you `Min` directly.
Remember the highest finished offset; it matters only when nothing is in flight.
template: foreach (var o in new long[] { 10, 11, 12, 13 }) dojoT.Started(o);
Dojo.Eq("12 is done but 10 is not: commit 10", (long?)10, dojoT.Committable);
Dojo.Eq("a new record in flight holds the position", (long?)14, dojoT.Committable);
Dojo.Eq("and moves on when it is done", (long?)15, dojoT.Committable);

steps.title: Sessions and message groups do this for you
body: The managed brokers move key-based dispatch into the broker:
```csharp
// Azure Service Bus: a session-enabled queue; one receiver owns a session at a time
await using var client = new ServiceBusClient("sb-shop.servicebus.windows.net", new DefaultAzureCredential());
await client.CreateSender("shipments").SendMessageAsync(new ServiceBusMessage(json) { SessionId = orderId, MessageId = eventId });
var processor = client.CreateSessionProcessor("shipments", new ServiceBusSessionProcessorOptions
MaxConcurrentSessions = 16,      // 16 orders in parallel, each one in order
AutoCompleteMessages = false,
processor.ProcessMessageAsync += async args => { await HandleAsync(args.Message); await args.CompleteMessageAsync(args.Message); };
processor.ProcessErrorAsync += args => { logger.LogError(args.Exception, "session error"); return Task.CompletedTask; };
await processor.StartProcessingAsync();
```csharp
// Amazon SQS FIFO: order per MessageGroupId, dedup per MessageDeduplicationId (5-minute window)
await sqs.SendMessageAsync(new SendMessageRequest
QueueUrl = shipmentsFifoUrl, MessageBody = json, MessageGroupId = orderId, MessageDeduplicationId = eventId,
- While a message of a group (or session) is being processed, the **rest of that group waits**; other groups flow.
Parallelism = the number of active groups, so a single group id for everything means one message at a time.
- A message that keeps failing blocks its group until the **max delivery count** (`MaxDeliveryCount` on Service Bus,
`maxReceiveCount` in the SQS redrive policy) moves it to the dead-letter queue.
- SQS FIFO throughput is limited per queue (300 API calls per second per action, more with batching and high
throughput mode), so pick group ids with many distinct values.

steps.prompt: A team moves to SQS FIFO and sets `MessageGroupId = "shipments"` on every message "to be safe". Twenty consumers poll the queue. What happens?
options: Only one message is processed at a time across all twenty consumers, because one group is delivered strictly in order
Twenty messages are processed in parallel, in order
SQS rejects the messages because the group id is not unique
Ordering is lost because there are twenty consumers
explain: FIFO order is per group, so one group means a single lane: the other nineteen consumers get nothing while a message of
the group is in flight. Use the entity id (`orderId`) as the group id: per-order order, many lanes in parallel.

steps.title: Simulate a key-dispatching consumer
prompt: Put the lesson together: dispatch one partition's records to workers by key and watch the commit position.
Write `List<string> Simulate(List<(long Offset, string Key, int Cost)> records, int workers)`. `Fnv1a` is given.
- A record goes to worker `Fnv1a(key) % workers`. All records are dispatched at time 0, in offset order.
- Each worker handles its records one after another, in offset order: a record finishes at the worker's previous
finish time + its `Cost` (the first one at `0 + Cost`).
- Go through the completions in order of finish time (equal times: lower offset first). After each one, the commit
position is the smallest offset not yet finished, or the last offset + 1 once everything is finished.
- Return one line per completion: `"t={finish} {key}@{offset} w{worker} commit {position}"`.
starter: // a stable 32-bit FNV-1a hash, given: never use string.GetHashCode() for routing
List<string> Simulate(List<(long Offset, string Key, int Cost)> records, int workers)
solution: // a stable 32-bit FNV-1a hash, given: never use string.GetHashCode() for routing

var done = new List<(long At, long Offset, string Key, int Worker)>();
foreach (var d in done.OrderBy(d => d.At).ThenBy(d => d.Offset))
